questions.q: According to this lesson, when is persistence (a scheduled task, service, or registry run key) an appropriate part of a test?
options: Whenever the tester personally judges it would be interesting to try
Never — persistence is always out of scope regardless of the engagement
Only when it's explicitly part of the signed scope, to simulate how a defender would notice and remove it
Only after the engagement has already officially ended
questions.explain: Persistence is treated like any other test artifact — permitted only when explicitly scoped, documented the moment it's created, and tied to the authorization that permits it.

questions.q: When should documentation of a created test artifact begin?
options: The moment the artifact is created, not reconstructed later from memory
Only after the client specifically asks for it
At the very end of the engagement, from memory
Documentation is optional if the artifact is removed quickly
questions.explain: The running log starts the moment an artifact is created — this is what makes verifiable cleanup possible and protects the tester if the client's own IR team finds something mid-engagement.

questions.q: Why does a documented log protect the tester if a client's incident response team discovers an unexplained artifact mid-engagement?
options: It doesn't — the tester has no real protection in that scenario
The log proves the artifact belongs to authorized testing activity, not a real intrusion
It transfers legal liability entirely to the client
It allows the tester to deny the artifact exists
questions.explain: A time-stamped, contemporaneous log is exactly what distinguishes authorized test activity from a real intrusion if anyone else discovers an artifact first.

questions.q: What is the correct way to verify cleanup is complete before an engagement closes?
options: Trust that memory of what was done is accurate
Skip verification if the engagement ran on schedule
Ask the client to verify it on their own
Cross-check every item against the running documentation log, one by one
questions.explain: Cleanup is verified against the documented log item by item, not reconstructed from memory — this is what makes the cleanup itself verifiable.

questions.q: Why is the audit trail of cleanup described as 'itself a deliverable'?
options: A client's security team needs that record to confirm their environment is back to its pre-test state
It's only useful for the tester's own personal records
Clients never actually read this part of a report
It has no connection to the chain-of-custody discipline from earlier in the course
questions.explain: The report explicitly documents what was created, when, and confirmation of removal, because the client's security team needs that record — closing the loop on the chain-of-custody discipline from Lesson 1.
